items.prompt: A primary API endpoint should receive traffic until it is unhealthy, then Route 53 should return the secondary. Which policy is the direct fit?
constraints: The primary and secondary have separate endpoints.
Health checks can observe the intended service health.
The secondary is ready to serve the workload.

options.text: Use Route 53 failover records with a primary and secondary role, health evaluation, and a tested secondary recovery path.
Use weighted records with 100% weight on the primary and call the weight a health check.
Use latency routing because it always chooses the primary until it fails.
Use two identical records without a routing policy so DNS clients choose the healthy endpoint automatically.

feedback.Reason: Failover routing expresses active-primary and passive-secondary behavior when health changes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route 53 evaluates the primary record's health and returns the secondary when the primary is unhealthy according to the configured policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team configures health checks, TTL, secondary capacity, and data readiness and tests the DNS response after primary impairment.
Details.errorCorrection: Weights control distribution, latency routing chooses based on latency rather than active-passive role, and unqualified duplicates are not a failover design.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DNS convergence and client caching limit failover speed, so the policy must be tested against the RTO.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Weights do not express health-based primary and secondary semantics by themselves.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Latency routing selects the lowest-latency healthy answer, not a fixed primary role.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Duplicate records without a deliberate policy do not provide deterministic failover behavior.

items.prompt: A server responds to TCP connections but returns an error page for every user request. Which health check is more meaningful for failover?
constraints: The endpoint is public or reachable by Route 53 health checks.
The check must represent usable application behavior.
The check must be safe and bounded.

options.text: Use an HTTP or HTTPS health check that validates a lightweight application readiness response and does not perform destructive business actions.
Use only a TCP check because an open port proves the application is healthy.
Use a full purchase transaction as the health check so every probe proves all business paths.
Return HTTP 200 from a static endpoint even when the application cannot serve users.

feedback.Reason: Failover health should represent user-serving readiness, not only a listening socket or an unsafe full transaction.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An application-aware check can detect an HTTP failure while remaining lightweight and free of side effects.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team separates local readiness from shared dependency alarms to avoid either routing to broken targets or causing failover storms.
Details.errorCorrection: TCP success does not prove HTTP behavior, probes should not charge users, and unconditional success hides the outage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep checks can detect more faults but increase probe load and correlated failure risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A listening port can serve an unhealthy application.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Health checks should be safe and not execute real business transactions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A permanently successful endpoint defeats failover detection.

items.prompt: A service claims a five-minute DNS failover objective but uses a one-hour TTL. What must be reconciled?
constraints: Resolvers and clients may cache answers.
The RTO includes routing convergence.
The secondary must be ready when clients switch.

options.text: Reconcile TTL, health-check detection, resolver behavior, client caching, and secondary readiness with the five-minute RTO; lower or redesign the bound if evidence requires it.
Keep the one-hour TTL because health checks force every client to query Route 53 immediately.
Change the DNS record every minute and assume all clients will honor the new value instantly.
Ignore DNS convergence because an RTO measures only the time to start the secondary.

feedback.Reason: DNS TTL and resolver caching are part of the failover path and can exceed the stated RTO.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Health detection changes authoritative answers, but cached answers remain in recursive resolvers and clients until their effective lifetime expires.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests real client and resolver behavior and includes DNS convergence in the recovery measurement.
Details.errorCorrection: Health checks do not invalidate every cache, record changes are not instant for all clients, and startup-only time omits routing delay.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower TTL increases query traffic and does not guarantee every client obeys it, so the architecture may need an application-level boundary too.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Resolvers can continue returning cached answers until TTL expires.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Clients and resolvers may not honor changes instantly despite frequent updates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS convergence is part of the end-to-end RTO when DNS is the client routing mechanism.

items.prompt: Users should normally reach the closest healthy Region, but the business wants a fixed primary and secondary for disaster recovery. Which routing policy is the better starting point?
constraints: The service is active-passive.
The secondary should not receive normal traffic.
Health determines when the secondary is returned.

options.text: Use failover routing rather than latency routing, because the requirement is an explicit primary and secondary relationship.
Use latency routing because it always honors the primary designation before considering distance.
Use weighted routing with equal weights because active-passive means equal distribution.
Use geolocation routing because country selection is equivalent to health-based failover.

feedback.Reason: Failover routing expresses active-passive intent, while latency, weighted, and geolocation policies serve different distribution goals.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Routing policy determines how Route 53 selects among records; health evaluation and primary-secondary roles must match the business behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The primary receives normal traffic and the secondary is returned when the primary is unhealthy according to the policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Latency chooses best latency, equal weights are active-active, and geolocation does not replace health failover.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Active-passive can waste standby capacity but simplifies write ownership and recovery semantics.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Latency routing is not an active-passive primary designation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Equal weights send normal traffic to both records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Geolocation maps users by location and does not express health-based primary failover.

items.prompt: A public application uses an ALB as its endpoint. Which Route 53 record integration should be evaluated?
constraints: The name should follow the ALB endpoint.
The ALB owns target health.
DNS should not require hard-coded IP updates.

options.text: Use an alias record to the ALB and rely on the load balancer's target health for the application path, adding Route 53 health logic only when a higher-level failover decision is required.
Create one A record for every current ALB IP and update it manually after every scaling event.
Point the record to a target instance IP so Route 53 can bypass the ALB during health failures.
Use a TXT record because text records automatically follow load-balancer addresses.

feedback.Reason: An alias to the load balancer follows its managed endpoint while target health remains owned by the ALB.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route 53 alias records integrate with supported AWS resources and avoid managing changing load-balancer addresses directly.
Details.scenarioApplication: The ALB handles target health and distribution; Route 53 handles the public name and any separate regional policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Manual IP records drift, direct target records bypass the intended health boundary, and TXT records do not route traffic.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If multi-Region failover is needed, the architect must layer a deliberate Route 53 policy above the regional load balancer.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Load-balancer addresses and scaling are managed and should not be copied manually into static records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Direct target records bypass load-balancer health and security behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: TXT records store text and are not a traffic-routing endpoint.

items.prompt: A new Region should receive 5% of traffic for validation, while the primary remains the normal destination. Which policy may fit?
constraints: The new Region is intentionally active.
The application can tolerate split traffic.
Write ownership and rollback behavior are defined.

options.text: Use weighted routing with monitored health and a controlled weight change, after proving data ownership and rollback behavior for split traffic.
Use failover routing because failover policies always send a chosen percentage to the secondary.
Use latency routing and assume it guarantees exactly 5% of requests.
Use equal weights without monitoring because both Regions are already production-ready.

feedback.Reason: Weighted routing expresses deliberate traffic percentages for canary or active-active use, unlike fixed primary-secondary failover.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Weights influence record selection, but health, resolver behavior, data consistency, and rollback remain part of the canary design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team increases weight gradually, measures errors and latency, and returns traffic to the primary if the new Region fails.
Details.errorCorrection: Failover does not provide a percentage split, latency does not guarantee an exact percentage, and equal weights are not a 5% canary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DNS weights are approximate across caches and clients, so the experiment must tolerate distribution variance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Failover is active-passive and not a percentage traffic policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Latency routing selects by measured latency and does not guarantee 5%.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Equal weights do not express a small canary and still require monitoring.

items.prompt: A failover Region is considered healthy only when its ALB, database, and critical dependency checks all pass. Which design can express this?
constraints: A single endpoint check is insufficient.
The combined health must avoid false positives.
The secondary must not be selected when a critical dependency is unusable.

options.text: Use a calculated or application-composed health signal that combines required checks with explicit thresholds, while keeping the checks safe and observable.
Use any one healthy static file as the regional health signal because one success proves all dependencies.
Require every optional analytics system to be healthy before serving core traffic.
Make the health endpoint depend on the primary Region so the secondary reports healthy only when the primary is healthy.

feedback.Reason: A composed health signal can represent the minimum conditions for serving the recovery workload without making it depend on unrelated or primary-only systems.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Health checks can be combined or surfaced through an application endpoint that reflects critical readiness and explicit thresholds.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests each dependency and the combined signal and avoids a health loop across Regions.
Details.errorCorrection: A static file misses dependencies, optional systems can unnecessarily block core service, and primary-dependent health defeats regional independence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deeper health increases detection fidelity but can create failover storms or dependency coupling if designed carelessly.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A static file does not prove data, network, or dependency readiness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Optional systems should not block the core objective without a stated requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A secondary health check cannot depend on the failed primary and still provide independent failover.

items.prompt: A private service uses an internal load balancer that Route 53 public health checkers cannot reach. What should the architect avoid?
constraints: The endpoint is private.
Public health checkers cannot enter the VPC directly.
The failover decision must use trustworthy health evidence.

options.text: Use a reachable health signal or an application-controlled health publication path appropriate for private resources, and validate the trust and staleness of that signal.
Assume Route 53 public checkers can always reach any private IP.
Make the internal load balancer public solely so a health check can run, without adding access controls.
Use the private IP as a health check target from the public internet and ignore the failed probes.

feedback.Reason: Health check placement must match endpoint reachability and must not be solved by unsafe public exposure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Private resources need a health signal from an appropriate reachable observer or a controlled calculated/application signal.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team protects the signal from forgery and staleness and tests what happens when the private service is unavailable.
Details.errorCorrection: Public checkers cannot automatically reach private IPs, making a private endpoint public increases exposure, and ignoring failed checks produces false health.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An application-published signal adds trust and freshness considerations that must be monitored.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Public health checkers do not have arbitrary access to private VPC endpoints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Making a private service public solely for monitoring expands its attack surface.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A failed probe is evidence that the selected observer cannot validate health, not a reason to ignore it.

items.prompt: The secondary Region's health endpoint calls the primary Region to compare data before returning healthy. Why is this dangerous?
constraints: The primary may be unavailable.
The secondary must make an independent failover decision.
Health checks should be bounded and nonrecursive.

options.text: The health check creates a cross-Region dependency and can make a healthy secondary appear unhealthy during the primary outage; use independent local readiness and data checks.
It improves failover because the secondary should never be healthy when the primary is down.
It is safe if the primary is called with a longer timeout so it has time to recover.
It removes the need for secondary data validation because the primary is the source of truth.

feedback.Reason: A recovery Region must not depend on the failed Region to advertise its own readiness.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent health checks avoid failover loops and preserve the ability to select a healthy secondary when the primary is unreachable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The secondary checks local capacity, data integrity, dependencies, and serving behavior without a primary network call.
Details.errorCorrection: Primary dependence creates false negatives, longer timeouts delay recovery, and a source-of-truth claim does not validate secondary readiness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent validation may require replicated metadata or local checks but is necessary for regional autonomy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A primary outage should not make the healthy secondary fail its own health check.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Longer timeout increases RTO and does not remove the dependency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The secondary still needs data and application validation before serving.

items.prompt: A failover record points to an ALB alias and the architect is unsure whether to attach a separate endpoint health check. What must be understood?
constraints: The alias target has its own health behavior.
The record policy may evaluate target health.
Double health checks can create unexpected failover behavior.

options.text: Understand the alias target's supported health evaluation and configure only the health logic needed for the regional or endpoint decision, then test unhealthy transitions.
Attach every possible health check because more checks always produce a more available answer.
Ignore health entirely because the ALB always routes to a healthy target even if the Region is unavailable.
Use a health check against one target IP and assume it represents the entire ALB and Region.

feedback.Reason: Route 53 and an alias target can each have health semantics, so the combined policy must be deliberate and tested.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Alias and target health evaluation can determine whether a record is eligible; an endpoint check may add a higher-level regional condition.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests ALB failure, target failure, Region failure, and the record returned in each case.
Details.errorCorrection: More checks can create false negatives, ignoring health can route to a failed Region, and one target is not always representative of the whole endpoint.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Health depth trades detection fidelity against complexity and failover flapping.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unnecessary checks can make a usable endpoint ineligible or cause flapping.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A regional or load-balancer failure can still make the alias unusable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One target check may not represent ALB, zone, data, or regional health.

items.prompt: A Route 53 failover record correctly selects the secondary, but users receive 503 responses after switching. What was not proven?
constraints: DNS routing changed as designed.
The secondary was not tested under production-like load.
The RTO includes application and dependency readiness.

options.text: Secondary application, data, credentials, quotas, downstream services, and capacity were not validated as part of the failover test.
The DNS record must be wrong because successful failover always proves the secondary is serving.
The TTL should be increased so the secondary has more time to return 503 responses.
The primary should remain in service even when health checks mark it unavailable.

feedback.Reason: DNS failover proves only answer selection; it does not create a ready application or data path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A secondary needs runtime artifacts, state, identity, network, quotas, capacity, and dependency behavior before it can serve.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team performs a full promotion test and records the actual end-to-end RTO rather than stopping at DNS resolution.
Details.errorCorrection: A correct DNS answer can point to an unready system, TTL does not repair 503s, and serving an unhealthy primary defeats failover.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keeping a warm standby costs more but reduces startup and validation time.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: DNS answer selection and application readiness are separate claims.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: TTL changes convergence, not application capacity or correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A failed primary should not continue receiving normal traffic under the failover policy.

items.prompt: The same health check is used both to route traffic and to page operators, but it is too shallow to diagnose the cause. What should change?
constraints: Routing needs a simple eligibility signal.
Operators need detailed diagnosis.
The checks must not cause a failover loop.

options.text: Keep the routing health signal focused on serving eligibility and add separate detailed metrics, alarms, logs, and traces for diagnosis and remediation.
Make the routing health check perform every diagnostic query on every probe.
Remove the routing health check and page operators after users report errors.
Use the database CPU alarm as the only application health signal.

feedback.Reason: Traffic eligibility and operator diagnosis have different depth and load requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A lightweight health signal can remove an unusable endpoint while independent telemetry explains why it is unhealthy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team avoids probe side effects and uses alarms and traces to find target, dependency, or data issues.
Details.errorCorrection: Heavy probes add load and can flap, user reports are too late, and database CPU misses edge or application failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate signals need correlation and ownership, but reduce health-check complexity and false failover.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Deep diagnostic probes can create load and correlated failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing health routing increases user impact before detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One database metric cannot represent full application serving health.

items.prompt: After a primary Region recovers, automatic failback would move traffic while its data is still catching up. What control is needed?
constraints: Primary recovery and data convergence are separate events.
Failback must not lose or conflict with writes.
The operator needs a controlled transition.

options.text: Use a controlled failback gate that requires primary data and dependency readiness, write ownership synchronization, and an observed promotion or rollback decision.
Automatically fail back as soon as the primary health endpoint returns HTTP 200.
Delete secondary data before failback so both Regions cannot disagree.
Split traffic evenly during convergence without defining write conflict behavior.

feedback.Reason: A healthy endpoint does not prove data convergence or safe return of write authority.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Failback requires synchronized state, capacity, routing, and ownership; a manual or automated gate can sequence those checks.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team freezes or coordinates writes as needed, verifies lag and dependencies, changes routing, and monitors rollback.
Details.errorCorrection: HTTP 200 can be too shallow, deleting data loses recovery state, and split writes require explicit conflict semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Controlled failback delays normalization but avoids a second outage or data conflict.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shallow health response does not prove data and ownership readiness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting recovery data is destructive and removes a safe fallback.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Split traffic during convergence can create conflicting writes and unclear authority.

items.prompt: A health endpoint reveals internal dependency details and accepts a user-supplied token. Which design is safer?
constraints: Health checks are external observers.
The endpoint should not expose secrets or internal topology.
The health signal must be hard to forge.

options.text: Expose a minimal safe readiness response, keep sensitive diagnostics in protected telemetry, and use network or application controls so the health result cannot be freely forged.
Return database credentials in the health body so operators can debug from Route 53.
Let any caller choose a token that makes the endpoint return healthy.
Include stack traces and private hostnames in every health response to maximize evidence.

feedback.Reason: Health endpoints are part of the external boundary and should expose only a safe eligibility signal, not secrets or forgeable state.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A minimal response supports routing while protected logs, metrics, and traces hold diagnostic detail and access control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests health behavior and observes detailed causes through operator channels rather than public responses.
Details.errorCorrection: Credentials, stack traces, and caller-controlled health outcomes create disclosure and failover manipulation risk.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A minimal health response may slow diagnosis, so independent protected telemetry is required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Health responses must not expose credentials.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Untrusted callers must not be able to force a healthy routing result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Stack traces and private names increase information exposure at the public boundary.

items.prompt: A health check alternates between healthy and unhealthy during brief dependency latency spikes, causing DNS failover flapping. What should be reviewed?
constraints: The service has transient latency.
Failover should not oscillate faster than recovery can stabilize.
The dependency and user objective remain important.

options.text: Tune timeout, interval, failure threshold, readiness behavior, and dependency protection from measured service objectives, and add stabilization or operator gates where needed.
Set the failure threshold to one and fail over on every transient slow response.
Ignore health failures so the primary remains preferred forever.
Add more DNS records with the same endpoint so flapping answers average out.

feedback.Reason: Health sensitivity must balance detection speed against false failover and stabilization behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Thresholds and intervals determine when transient failures change record eligibility; dependency-aware readiness prevents probe storms.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests intermittent latency and selects values that meet RTO without repeated route changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Threshold one increases false failover, ignoring failures hides outages, and duplicate records do not average a bad policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Slower detection can increase RTO, while aggressive detection can cause flapping; measurements set the trade-off.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single transient failure can create unnecessary failover and user churn.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Ignoring failed health checks defeats the purpose of failover.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Duplicate records do not correct health thresholds or stabilize the endpoint.

items.prompt: Which test provides the strongest evidence for Route 53 failover?
constraints: The primary must be impaired safely.
The secondary must be ready.
DNS convergence and application success are both in scope.

options.text: Induce a controlled primary health failure, observe authoritative and real resolver answers, measure client convergence and application RTO, then restore through a controlled failback.
Change the record in a local hosts file and call failover validated.
Check only that Route 53 displays the primary as unhealthy.
Test the secondary without impairing the primary or changing routing.

feedback.Reason: Failover evidence must include health detection, DNS propagation, client behavior, secondary serving, and recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The full path exposes TTL, resolver, capacity, application, data, and failback gaps that console status alone cannot show.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records timing and correctness at each stage and updates the runbook from observed behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: A local hosts file bypasses DNS, console health does not prove client or service recovery, and secondary-only testing omits transition behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Controlled failure tests require safety and rollback controls but validate the actual RTO.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A local override does not exercise Route 53, resolver caching, or client convergence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Control-plane health does not prove end-to-end failover.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A ready secondary is necessary but not sufficient without a transition test.

items.prompt: A failover record points users to a secondary that has no equivalent authorization or WAF controls. What is the architecture risk?
constraints: The secondary must preserve security policy.
Users may arrive through the same public name.
Data and credentials are sensitive.

options.text: The secondary is not a valid failover target until identity, TLS, WAF, origin access, network, secrets, logging, and data protections match the required security contract.
Security can be added after failover because availability always takes priority over authorization.
Use a different public domain so the secondary can use weaker controls without affecting the primary.
Disable TLS at the secondary because DNS already proves the request is trusted.

feedback.Reason: Failover must preserve the service's security boundary; routing users to an unprotected copy creates a security incident.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The secondary needs equivalent identity, transport, network, data, and observability controls before it can serve the public name.
Details.scenarioApplication: The failover runbook validates security artifacts and policies before promotion and tests direct-origin bypass.
Details.errorCorrection: Availability does not justify unauthorized access, a different domain changes user and policy behavior, and DNS is not trust authentication.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Duplicating security controls adds governance and rotation work but is required for a safe standby.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Failover to an unprotected system trades an outage for a security breach.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A different domain can break client policy and does not make weak controls acceptable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS resolution does not encrypt or authenticate application traffic.

items.prompt: Which evidence is strongest for approving DNS-based regional failover?
constraints: The RTO includes DNS and client convergence.
The secondary has data and application capacity.
Health and security behavior must be tested.

options.text: A controlled primary impairment showing health detection, authoritative and recursive DNS behavior, client convergence, secondary correctness, security, capacity, and measured RTO.
A screenshot of two Route 53 records with primary and secondary labels.
A low DNS TTL without a secondary application test.
A successful health check from one probe location while the application remains untested.

feedback.Reason: DNS failover is an end-to-end claim, so evidence must cover routing, convergence, secondary readiness, security, and recovery time.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A failure exercise measures the actual path from health detection to user-serving recovery and reveals hidden dependencies.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records RTO, RPO, failback, resolver, and application behavior and retains a runbook tied to evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Labels and TTL alone do not prove recovery, and one health probe cannot validate all users or application dependencies.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DNS failover can be cost-effective but has convergence limits that may require additional application routing or client behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Record labels do not prove health, convergence, or secondary serving.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: TTL is one parameter and cannot replace an end-to-end test.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One probe does not prove application behavior or global client convergence.
